title: Array, typed arrays, and array-like objects
hook: JavaScript Array is a dynamic object with a length property and prototype methods — not a fixed buffer like C# arrays. Typed arrays (Int32Array, Uint8Array) back binary data and share ArrayBuffer memory with zero-copy views.

blocks.text: **Array** stores ordered values with auto-growing **length**. Indices are string keys internally (`"0"`, `"1"`). **Typed arrays** are views over **ArrayBuffer** — fixed element size, no push/pop on buffer itself. **Array-like** objects have length and indexed properties but lack Array.prototype methods (NodeList, arguments in non-arrow functions). **Spread** `[...arrayLike]` or `Array.from` converts to real arrays.

entries.plainDefinition: Ordered mutable collection with length and prototype methods.
Raw binary memory allocation; not directly indexed.
Int32Array, Float64Array, etc. — typed view over buffer bytes.
Has length and [index] but not Array.isArray.

blocks.text: Choosing Array vs typed array affects performance for WebGL, audio, and file parsing. Sparse arrays (holes) skip indices in iteration — map skips holes. C# `T[]` and `List<T>` are homogeneous; JS Array mixes types. `array.length = 0` clears without reallocating identity — useful for reusable buffers in hot loops.

blocks.title: Array.isArray
blocks.body: instanceof Array fails across iframes — use Array.isArray(x) for reliable check.

snippet.label: Sparse arrays and holes
snippet.code:
const sparse = [1, , 3]; // hole at index 1
console.log(sparse.length); // 3
console.log(1 in sparse);     // false

sparse.forEach((v, i) => console.log(i, v)); // skips index 1
console.log([...sparse]); // [1, undefined, 3] — map fills hole
snippet.explanation: Hole is not undefined element — missing property. forEach skips; spread converts hole to undefined.

snippet.label: Array-like to Array
snippet.explanation: Array.from and spread copy indexed values into real Array with full prototype methods.

snippet.label: Typed array over buffer
snippet.explanation: Int32Array and Uint8Array alias same memory — endianness matters when sharing with network.

snippet.label: Failure mode — length as security
snippet.explanation: Setting length from untrusted input can allocate huge sparse arrays — validate bounds.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using for...in on arrays — iterates keys including enumerable props. Assuming map visits holes. Confusing Array and typed array — typed arrays have fixed length. Trusting array.length from user input. Using new Array(n) when meaning [n] — creates sparse length-n array.

blocks.text: V8 optimizes **packed** arrays (dense indices) differently from **holey** arrays — performance cliffs when deleting middle elements or using new Array(large). **O(n) shift/unshift** on large arrays — use deque pattern or linked structure. **ArrayBuffer** is transferable to Workers with zero copy. Know **MAX_SAFE_INTEGER** for numeric indices. **flat** depth and **Array.fromAsync** for async iterables in modern code.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain hole vs undefined element. Says Array is fixed-size like C# array. Unaware typed arrays share ArrayBuffer.

interviewTakeaways: Array is object with length; indices are property keys.
Sparse holes: forEach skips; spread maps hole to undefined.
TypedArray views share ArrayBuffer — binary interop.
60s: Dynamic JS Array vs C# List. Holes. TypedArray for binary. Array.from for array-like. Validate length from user.
commonPitfalls: Weak: "Array and typed array are the same." Strong: "Array is generic object; typed array is fixed-width view over ArrayBuffer."
Weak: "for...in is fine for arrays." Strong: "Use for...of or forEach — for...in includes enumerable properties."
Strong: "Explain hole at index 1 — in operator false, spread yields undefined."

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript Array<T> is compile-time only; run time is untyped JS Array unless typed arrays.
C# List<T> is generic homogeneous; JS Array holds any element type at run time.
